title: Rocketdyne Returns, UK Picks Portuguese Drone Over Watchkeeper, AI Flies 27 Intercepts
subhead: AE Industrial relaunches the historic Rocketdyne brand as a standalone space propulsion company, the UK awards a £400M surveillance drone contract to TEKEVER, and Lockheed's Skunk Works demonstrates AI-controlled air-to-air intercepts using infrared sensor data.

sections.heading: Rocketdyne Reborn as L3Harris Completes Space Propulsion Split
sections.body:
AE Industrial Partners finalized its $845 million acquisition of L3Harris Technologies' space propulsion, power, and electronics units on August 4, relaunching the historic Rocketdyne brand as an independent company for the first time in over two decades. AE Industrial holds a 60% controlling stake; L3Harris retains a 40% noncontrolling minority interest.

The deal is a deliberate bifurcation of American propulsion capabilities. The new Rocketdyne takes the RL10 upper-stage engine, in-space electric propulsion thrusters, nuclear power systems for spacecraft, and space electronics — employing roughly 1,300 people across five U.S. locations. What stays with L3Harris is the military side: the RS-25 engine that powers NASA's Space Launch System core stage, solid rocket motors, and hypersonic propulsion systems. L3Harris is separately preparing a public offering of its Missile Solutions business for mid-2027 after delaying from its original second-half 2026 target, according to Breaking Defense.

The transaction reverses decades of consolidation. Rocketdyne's lineage stretches to 1955 under North American Aviation, powering the Saturn V and Space Shuttle main engines before passing through Rockwell, Boeing, Pratt & Whitney, Aerojet, and finally L3Harris's 2023 acquisition of Aerojet Rocketdyne for $4.7 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: The split separates civil space propulsion from military missile hardware under different ownership structures and investment timelines — a private-equity-controlled Rocketdyne versus a publicly traded L3Harris keeping war-fighting propulsion. For procurement officials, it means a new phone number for RL10 engines and a different corporate parent making long-term investment decisions about America's upper-stage launch capability.

sections.heading: UK Ditches Watchkeeper for TEKEVER's AR5 in £400M Deal
sections.body:
The UK Ministry of Defence has selected Portuguese firm TEKEVER to deliver CORVUS, the British Army's new surveillance capability, replacing the troubled Watchkeeper program. The contract is worth up to £400 million over ten years, sustaining and creating hundreds of skilled jobs across TEKEVER's UK operations.

Built on TEKEVER's battle-proven AR5 platform, CORVUS carries up to 50 kg of surveillance payloads including cameras and sensors, providing persistent round-the-clock intelligence gathering. The system introduces what TEKEVER calls a 'continuous capability evolution' model, allowing emerging technologies and battlefield lessons to be rapidly integrated under full UK sovereign control — a direct contrast to the fixed-specification Watchkeeper program that plagued the Army for over a decade.

Production will be centered at TEKEVER's new manufacturing facility in Swindon, with engineering in Bristol and Southampton, and testing in West Wales. A consortium of UK SMEs will support the supply chain. The AR5 draws on over 50,000 operational flight hours in Ukraine since 2022. The capability is expected to begin entering service later this year, subject to final contract signature.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a significant shift in European UAV procurement: a mid-size Portuguese company beating established defense primes for a major NATO army's ISR platform. The UK is betting on a commercial-off-the-shelf platform with combat pedigree over a bespoke, over-budget national program — and using a continuous-upgrade contract model that could become the template for future European defense procurements.

sections.heading: Skunk Works Flies AI-Controlled Intercepts Using IRST Sensor Data
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works and the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School revealed on August 4 that the X-62 VISTA variable in-flight simulation test aircraft completed 27 autonomous intercepts of airborne targets across eight flights in April 2026, using AI agents fed by a Legion Pod Infrared Search and Track (IRST) sensor.

The milestones were achieved under two accelerated test programs, HAVE HEAT and HAVE HOLIDAYS. During HAVE HEAT, the X-62 tracked a live T-38 Talon with the IRST pod, then fed that data to an AI agent that autonomously piloted the fighter into tactical intercept positions. Skunk Works said its 'Supermassive' AI agent generation capability was integrated and ground-tested in just three months.

Lt. Col. Joshua Strafaccia, dean of faculty for research at the Air Force Test Pilot School, said HAVE HEAT 'bridges a capability gap and positions us to test advanced autonomy faster.' Ron Fehlen, VP and general manager of Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, called it 'a decisive advance toward delivering AI-augmented air dominance for the United States.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first demonstrated closing of the sensor-to-action loop with an AI agent flying a real combat aircraft against live targets using infrared data — not simulated, not GPS-based, but IRST-passive-sensor-driven. The three-month integration timeline for Supermassive also signals how fast the AI agent development cycle is compressing. The implication for future air combat: AI copilots that can autonomously detect, track, and intercept threats using passive sensors, without emitting radar.

sections.heading: Ukraine Sends 320 Drones Against Russia in Single Night Wave
sections.body:
Russian air defenses reported intercepting and destroying 320 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russian regions in a single overnight attack spanning August 3–4, according to the Russian Defense Ministry. The drones targeted 18 regions including Moscow, Leningrad, Belgorod, Bryansk, and Crimea — one of the widest geographic footprints of any Ukrainian drone assault to date.

In the Moscow Region, five people were killed and ten injured, with the Chekhov district hit hardest. Fires broke out in an industrial zone in Novoselki, damaging a warehouse, a power substation, and an administrative building, according to Governor Andrey Vorobyov. In the Leningrad Region, a drone struck a Wildberries logistics facility near Krasny Bor, injuring one person and triggering evacuation. Wildberries also reported damage to a warehouse near Tver.

The sheer scale — 320 drones across 18 regions in one wave — illustrates the continued escalation in drone warfare volume on both sides, even as ground front lines remain relatively static.
sections.whyItMatters: The 320-drone wave represents a new benchmark for single-night drone attack volume in the Russia-Ukraine war. The geographic spread to 18 regions, including strikes near Moscow and St. Petersburg logistics hubs, signals Ukraine's increasing ability to project drone power across all of European Russia. For defense planners worldwide, this validates the thesis that mass drone attacks have become a core — not peripheral — capability, reinforcing demand for layered counter-drone systems.

sections.heading: Pentagon Launches Counter-Drone Marketplace as War Demand Soars
sections.body:
The Pentagon's counter-drone task force JIAFT-401 and software company Kaizen Laboratories have launched the Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Marketplace, an online platform designed to let military buyers, federal agencies, and law enforcement rapidly discover, evaluate, and purchase validated counter-drone technologies. Kaizen was awarded a $15 million contract in May to build and operate the platform.

Built in under nine weeks using Kaizen's proprietary Blacksmith development environment, the marketplace allows users to search by tactical requirements, compare performance data, and submit acquisition requests — effectively turning C-UAS procurement into an e-commerce-style experience. An AI-powered 'Capability Planner' lets operators describe a threat in plain language and receive assembled recommendations across the kill chain. Vendors including Anduril and AeroVironment are already listed.

The platform is modeled on Ukraine's Brave1 Market and directly addresses the cost asymmetry exposed by the Iran war: the U.S. and allies have expended large numbers of expensive missiles shooting down cheap Iranian Shahed drones. Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401, called drones 'a defining threat of our time' and said the marketplace will 'share best practices and equipment globally,' including via foreign military sales channels.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a structural shift in Pentagon procurement philosophy — bypassing traditional acquisition timelines by creating an app-store model for counter-drone tech. The nine-week build time and $15M price tag are a fraction of traditional defense software contracts. If it works, the marketplace model could expand beyond C-UAS into other fast-evolving technology areas where the threat moves faster than the acquisition cycle.

sections.heading: Japan's Defense White Paper Declares Combat Drones Essential, Flags China Carrier Threat
sections.body:
Japan's Cabinet adopted its annual defense white paper on August 4, a 598-page document that declares combat drones 'essential' to Japan's defense strategy and identifies China as the country's 'biggest strategic challenge.' Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called speed the top priority, and the Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency has already selected four drone makers from 38 applicants for a rapid development program with naval testing this month.

Toshiba announced on August 1 that it will jointly develop combat drones with startup Pro Drone, signaling a shift among Japan's traditional conglomerates toward arms production. The paper warns that Japan's commercial drone market remains heavily dependent on Chinese imports — a vulnerability the government aims to address by building indigenous capability.

On China, the white paper flags the December 2025 fire-control radar lock on Japanese aircraft during Chinese carrier drills near southwestern Japan, and the unprecedented deployment of two Chinese carriers near Iwo Jima in June. It also describes North Korea's hypersonic missile program as an 'increasingly serious and pressing threat.' On the industrial side, the paper pledges greater investment in Japan's defense industrial base, including support for startups, and highlights recent relaxations of arms export rules — including an agreement to jointly develop and supply 11 upgraded Mogami-class frigates to Australia and transfers of retired destroyers to the Philippines.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan's white paper marks an acceleration of the country's break from pacifist defense norms — not just in rhetoric but in procurement decisions and industrial policy. The four-maker drone rapid development program, Toshiba's entry into combat drones, and the Mogami-class frigate export deal with Australia all point to a Japan that is building, exporting, and fielding military hardware at a pace inconceivable five years ago. The radar-lock incident with China and the Iwo Jima carrier deployment add urgency.

sections.heading: Palantir Surges on 'Otherworldly' Commercial Revenue, Europe Pushes Back
sections.body:
Palantir Technologies raised its full-year revenue forecast to as much as $8.16 billion after posting second-quarter results that CEO Alex Karp described as 'otherworldly.' U.S. commercial sales surged 149% year-over-year to $764 million, well above analyst estimates of $716 million. Palantir now projects up to $4.91 billion in adjusted operating income for the year. Its market value has more than doubled since late 2024 to roughly $300 billion.

The commercial surge contrasts sharply with the company's European government business, where officials in France and the UK have moved to end deals with Palantir, citing tech sovereignty concerns. Karp acknowledged the divide, telling analysts that growth in Europe 'sucks' and that the company sometimes makes decisions 'against our economic interests' by supporting European institutions. Overall international sales grew just 33% to $362.5 million — a fraction of the 115% U.S. revenue growth to $1.57 billion.

Karp also pushed back against the threat of AI model-makers displacing Palantir, saying customers have declined to become 'vassal states of the language labs' and positioning Palantir as a model-agnostic platform that allows switching between AI providers. Palantir shares rose as much as 15% in after-hours trading.
sections.whyItMatters: Palantir's divergence — booming U.S. commercial demand versus a European market actively trying to replace it — is becoming the sharpest illustration of the transatlantic tech sovereignty divide. The 149% U.S. commercial growth rate shows that Palantir is winning the domestic AI platform battle, but the European pushback on sovereignty grounds could set a template for how other U.S. defense tech firms get treated across the EU.

bottomLine: Three developments signal where defense procurement is heading. Rocketdyne's rebirth as a standalone company under private equity separates America's civil space propulsion from its missile business — and the different investment horizons that come with each. The UK's £400M TEKEVER deal and the Pentagon's C-UAS Marketplace both demonstrate a growing appetite for commercial-off-the-shelf speed over bespoke defense programs. And Lockheed's AI intercept milestone, Japan's combat drone white paper, and Palantir's commercial surge all underscore the same reality: the companies and countries that can compress development and procurement timelines fastest are gaining the edge, whether in AI, drones, or defense software.
